clue.text: Sat before fantastic Sunday lunch?

indicators.note: something fantastic is fanciful and unreal, so the letters are reworked into a fanciful new order

blocks.note: both words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone sat down in good time for a marvellous Sunday lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sat before' reads as when you took your seat, but those nine letters are the raw material. The question mark flags that the definition is by example.
explanation.definitionFit: The roast joint of beef is the classic British Sunday family meal, so it is one example of such a dinner.

clue.text: Ply that’s cut very fine

indicators.note: a word that has been cut is shortened, so it loses its final letter

blocks.note: to ply someone with food and drink is to regale them

explanation.surface: Plywood sliced so thinly it is almost nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ply' looks like the noun for a layer of wood, but it is the verb, to keep supplying someone with food or drink; dock the last letter of that synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Regal means fit for a king, magnificent and splendid, which is how something very fine looks.

clue.text: One that could — or couldn’t? — bring to mind a riddle?

definitions.text: One that could — or couldn’t? — bring to mind a riddle?

blocks.clueFragment: One that could — or couldn’t? — bring to mind a riddle?
blocks.note: surface reading: something able, or perhaps unable, to call up a puzzling riddle
setter's reading: a riddle is also a coarse sieve, and a forgetful mind is compared to one

explanation.walkthrough: Riddle here is the old word for a garden sieve. A forgetful person's mind is said to be like one because everything falls through, hence it may or may not bring things to mind.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone forgetful whose recollections leak away like water through mesh, so their recall is unreliable.

clue.text: Shot played by Ashes batter, maybe, evaluating spin

definitions.text: Shot played by Ashes batter, maybe

blocks.clueFragment: Shot played by Ashes batter, maybe
blocks.note: first meaning: a drive (a straight attacking stroke) hit in a Test match, as an Ashes game is
second meaning: a trial run in a car before buying it

explanation.surface: A cricket commentator judges how well an England batter handles spin bowling.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ashes is the England v Australia Test series in cricket, and a drive is a batting stroke. 'Spin' sounds like bowling but is a short ride in a car.
explanation.definitionFit: A test-drive is a trial run in a vehicle to judge how it performs, so evaluating a car while taking a short ride.

clue.text: Quickly twisted sad news from journal’s head office?

blocks.note: ED is short for editor, the head of a journal's office
a death is sad news

explanation.surface: A newspaper's grim announcement from the top office, swiftly spun.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay reads as a headline: the editor died. That is the sad news from the head office.
explanation.definitionFit: Water that eddied swirled round in rapid circular currents, turning on itself fast.

clue.text: Energy provider, very good one, in food: ham, perhaps

indicators.note: one thing set in another sits inside it, so the outer word wraps around

blocks.note: a saint is a very good person, abbreviated ST
fare is food served
a ham is an overacting actor

explanation.surface: A list of things that give energy: something excellent, a food such as ham.
explanation.walkthrough: Ham looks like food on the list but is a hammy performer. ST for saint is the usual crossword 'good one'.
explanation.definitionFit: A fast reactor is a type of nuclear reactor generating electrical power, so it supplies the grid.

clue.text: Defiant bachelor: nothing can stop what he is!

indicators.note: a stopper plugs a gap from within, so these letters plug the middle of another word

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for bachelor
O looks like zero
a bachelor is unmarried

explanation.surface: A stubborn single man boasts nothing will stop him staying single.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What he is' points back at the bachelor: he is unmarried.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone unbowed has not bent the knee or submitted, remaining resistant and undaunted.

clue.text: New Year turned lively in square

indicators.note: lively things jump about, so the letters are jumbled into another order

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for new
Y is the abbreviation for year
taken as written

explanation.surface: Revellers turned out in their thousands to see in the New Year in a town square.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Square' looks like the place of the party, but it is the definition in its sense of old-fashioned.
explanation.definitionFit: A square person is conventional and out of touch with fashion, the opposite of hip or cool.

clue.text: There’s a case for butter, and one having more chocolate?

indicators.note: a case is the outside of something, so only the outer letters of the word are kept

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word
one having something is its owner

explanation.surface: An argument for butter, and for someone who likes extra chocolate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More chocolate' is a comparative of the colour, not a quantity of sweets: chocolate as a shade of brown.
explanation.definitionFit: Chocolate is a dark brown shade, so something more chocolate in colour is darker brown.

clue.text: Being left by Dutch with passport, maybe, one in red headpiece

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for with
a passport is one example of identification
someone in the red owes money, so is an ower
a hood covers the head

explanation.surface: Someone leaves the Dutch border with a passport and red hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dutch' here is old Cockney slang for a wife (my old Dutch), not someone from the Netherlands; being left by her through death makes a man a widower.
explanation.definitionFit: Widowerhood is the condition of a man whose wife has died, so he has been bereft of his spouse.

clue.text: Old tyrant’s sins you and I’d laid out

indicators.note: things laid out are spread and arranged afresh, so the letters are set in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, joined by 'and'
the contraction without its apostrophe

explanation.surface: A confession that an ancient despot's crimes were set out for all to see.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after 'tyrant' is 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Dionysius the Elder was the ruthless ruler of Syracuse in ancient Sicily, a byword for despotic cruelty.

clue.text: One next to do lively dance for a change

blocks.note: in the sol-fa scale do is followed by re
a jig is a brisk folk dance

explanation.surface: A partner at a party joins in a lively dance for something different.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' is not the verb but the first note of do-re-mi, and the note next to it is the one wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A rejig is an informal word for a rearrangement or reorganisation, a modest alteration.

clue.text: Centre for trek, facility across lake, is free

indicators.note: the centre is the middle, so only the middle letters of the word are kept

blocks.note: the two middle letters of the four
L is the abbreviation for lake
to do something with facility is to do it with ease

explanation.surface: A walking-holiday base, with amenities beside the lake, costs nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Facility' sounds like a building at the centre, but it means effortlessness. It sits next to the lake letter rather than wrapping it.
explanation.definitionFit: To free a captive is to let them go, to liberate them from confinement.

clue.text: You must stop pilgrimage after upsetting ancient tribe

indicators.note: a stopper sits inside an opening, so one piece is placed within another
in a down entry, upsetting tips a word up so it reads from the bottom

blocks.note: the hadj is the Muslim pilgrimage to Mecca
U is text-speak for you

explanation.surface: A warning that someone must halt a pilgrimage after it has upset an ancient people.
explanation.walkthrough: The pilgrimage is the hadj, also spelt hajj; turned up it reads JDAH, then the letter for you plugs it.
explanation.definitionFit: Judah was one of the twelve tribes of Israel, descended from a son of Jacob in the Bible.

clue.text: Facts are put up on register — for polymath?

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting a word up raises it so it reads bottom to top

blocks.note: gen is British slang for information
taken as written
a register is a list

explanation.surface: Data is posted on a list of names, perhaps to find a person of wide learning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gen' is British slang for the facts or the lowdown. 'On' in a down clue puts the reversed word above the register.
explanation.definitionFit: A generalist has knowledge across many fields rather than one specialism, as a polymath does, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Fancied rogue’s seductive embraces

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold within the arms, so the phrase holds the word inside it

blocks.note: running across the two words

explanation.surface: A rakish charmer's seductive hugs were much desired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancied' looks like the reaction to the rogue's hugs, but it is the definition in its sense of supposed.
explanation.definitionFit: To fancy that something is so is to suppose or imagine it, to conjecture without certainty.

clue.text: Start a fight

blocks.note: first meaning: to begin working in earnest
second meaning: a scrap or brawl

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as an instruction to pick a fight; split it into two meanings of one hyphenated phrase, verb and noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means begin vigorously, and the noun is a brief quarrel or bout of fisticuffs.

clue.text: Make portent involving youth predicting disaster

indicators.note: to involve is to wrap something in, so one word surrounds another

blocks.note: to do is to make
an omen is a portent
a lad is a youth

explanation.surface: Someone concocts a dark warning about a young person who foresees catastrophe.
explanation.walkthrough: DO for 'make' sits in front, then the omen wraps around the youth.
explanation.definitionFit: Something doom-laden is heavy with foreboding, full of gloomy forecasts of catastrophe.

clue.text: Old PM was familiar with pop song

blocks.note: David Lloyd George was British Prime Minister 1916 to 1922
to be familiar with someone is to know them
pop is what you call your own father

explanation.surface: A former Prime Minister turns out to have known a pop song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' looks like pop music but is Dad. The title is a well-known British rugby and army song sung to the tune of Onward, Christian Soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a comic British singalong, a ditty chanted on terraces and in barracks, so it is a song.

clue.text: Hamper: medium one, not large, is in fashion

indicators.note: 'not' says something is absent, so one letter is taken away
to be in something is to sit inside it, so letters are placed within another word

blocks.note: style is fashion
L is the abbreviation for large
M is the clothing-size abbreviation for medium
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Clothes sizes: a medium, never a large, is what is fashionable in a basket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hamper' looks like a picnic basket noun, but it is the verb. The sizes M and L are swapped in effect: lose the large and put medium plus one in.
explanation.definitionFit: To stymie someone is to obstruct or thwart their progress, to impede and frustrate them.

clue.text: Group heading for Scotland Yard

indicators.note: the heading is what comes at the top, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter
a quad, or quadrangle, is a yard enclosed by buildings

explanation.surface: A team of detectives sets off for Scotland Yard, the London police headquarters.
explanation.walkthrough: Scotland Yard reads as one place but splits in two; 'Yard' is a courtyard.
explanation.definitionFit: A squad is a small team of people, such as police officers or players, working as a unit.

clue.text: Rambler getting stick before run

blocks.note: a wand is a thin stick
ere is a poetic word for before
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A hiker picks up a walking stick before setting off at a run.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' is not an order instruction but a word in its own right: the old ERE.
explanation.definitionFit: A rambler is someone who walks for pleasure across the country, roaming about without fixed purpose.

clue.text: I note there’s little room outside section of glacier

indicators.note: lying outside something means surrounding it, so one word goes round the other

blocks.note: taken as written
fa is the fourth note of the sol-fa scale
a cell is a small room

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a cramped hut sits beside part of a glacier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' is a musical note from do-re-mi, not a remark.
explanation.definitionFit: An icefall is the steep, broken stretch of a glacier where it tumbles over a drop, like a frozen waterfall.

clue.text: Hitch or take plane home, stopping at hotel on time — ten — surprisingly

indicators.note: something that turns out surprisingly is unexpected, so the letters land in an unexpected order
to stop a gap is to plug it, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: to fly in is to arrive home by air
taken as written
H is Hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A traveller hitchhikes or flies home, checking in at a hotel at ten sharp to everyone's surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hitch' looks like hitchhiking alongside taking a plane, but it is the definition, a snag. 'Or' merely offers it as an alternative name for the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a small flaw that spoils something otherwise good, so it is a snag or drawback.

clue.text: Inclined unfortunately to promote surfing primarily before books

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter is kept
promoting moves something up the ranks, so a letter is lifted out and set higher in the word

blocks.note: alas is said when something is unfortunate
the opening letter
NT is the New Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: Surfing is going downhill, perhaps; a promoter is inclined to push it ahead of reading.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the exclamation for 'unfortunately', then move its S, named by surfing's first letter, up one place in the down entry before adding the books.
explanation.definitionFit: Aslant means at a slope or angle, leaning over obliquely rather than standing upright.

clue.text: Bath for one to lie in really after one’s dropped temperature

indicators.note: something dropped is let go, so a letter is left out
to be in something is to sit inside it, so one word is placed within another

blocks.note: a unit is a single one; the 's stands for has
T is the abbreviation for temperature
where a thing sits is where it lies
very is used to mean really, as in very good

explanation.surface: Someone lingers in a hot bath until it cools down.
explanation.walkthrough: Bath is the English city with a university, not the tub; the 's after 'one' is 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: The University of Bath is one example of a British higher-education institution, hence 'for one'.

clue.text: Stories being spread of a coup, ultimately baseless

indicators.note: something spread is scattered about, so the letters are dispersed into a new order
ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
the final letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: Groundless rumours are circulating about an attempted overthrow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Baseless' looks like a judgement on the rumours, but its eight letters go into the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesop's fables are the classic ancient Greek collection of short moral tales with animal characters.

clue.text: Old flame put out

blocks.note: an old flame is a former partner
to put a question is to pose it

explanation.surface: An old sweetheart's torch has been extinguished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' reads as extinguished, fitting a flame, but the phrase splits: 'put' is wordplay and 'out' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To out someone is to reveal their secret publicly, which is to uncover or unmask them.

clue.text: Each to come up

blocks.note: first meaning: per person, so much apiece
second meaning: still in the future, coming up

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense needs a space: 'a head' means per person. Read whole, it means in the future.
explanation.definitionFit: Events still in front of us in time are yet to happen, and charging per person is charging per capita.

clue.text: Clues roughened up for the solver originally show the setter can win!

indicators.note: originally means at the start, so only each word's opening letter is kept

blocks.clueFragment: Clues roughened up for the solver
blocks.note: the opening letters of six words

explanation.surface: A crossword compiler gloats that toughened clues will beat the solver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The setter' looks like the crossword compiler but is the dog breed, such as an Irish setter. CRUFTS is Britain's famous annual dog show.
explanation.definitionFit: Crufts is the big British dog show, where a pedigree gundog breed like the Irish setter can take Best in Show.

clue.text: When turning blue, tip of tongue was hanging out

indicators.note: something turning faces about, so the word is read backwards
a tip is the very end, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: blue jokes are smutty, lewd ones
the opening letter

explanation.surface: Someone gasping for breath, going blue, with the tongue lolling out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue' looks like a colour but means risqué. 'Hanging out' looks like the tongue lolling but means living somewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: To dwell somewhere is to live or stay there, so someone who dwelt was residing or hanging about.

clue.text: High state of versatility — role-player’s content!

indicators.note: a thing's content is what lies inside it, so the word is found within the phrase

blocks.note: running across the two words

explanation.surface: An actor delights in the peak of versatility.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High state' sounds like a mood, but it is a mountainous region.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tyrol is an Alpine province in western Austria, mountainous and so lofty.

clue.text: Tune that’s simple and sweet — a heaven-sent relief?

blocks.note: an air is a simple melody
a drop is a small boiled sweet, such as a lemon drop

explanation.surface: A simple sweet melody feels like a godsend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heaven-sent' is literal: the relief comes down from the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: An airdrop delivers supplies by parachute from aircraft, so aid literally descends from the sky to people in need.

clue.text: Worn out after month dealing with excavation

blocks.note: DEC is the calendar abbreviation for December
re means concerning
a pit is a dug hole

explanation.surface: A digger is exhausted after a month working on an excavation.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition 'Worn out' sits first, and 'after' places the rest behind the month.
explanation.definitionFit: Decrepit describes something dilapidated or a person enfeebled by age, worn out by long use.

clue.text: Car’s exterior showing this off?

blocks.note: surface reading: a car's bodywork showing off something about it
setter's reading: the shiny plated trim that a gleaming vehicle flaunts on its outside

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks a cryptic description: what does the outside of a flashy car show off? Its bright metal trim, bumpers and grille.
explanation.definitionFit: Chromium plating on bumpers and trim is the gleaming metal finish that classic motors flaunt.

clue.text: Despot’s wife moving a way back

indicators.note: going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the letters read in reverse

blocks.note: astir means up and moving about
taken as written
ST is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: A tyrant's spouse is moving house, going back some way.
explanation.walkthrough: The despot is a Russian tsar, so his wife is the tsarina, here in a rarer spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A tsaritsa was the consort of a tsar, the autocratic emperor of Russia.

clue.text: Targets relatives and friends

blocks.note: aunts are relatives
allies are friends

explanation.surface: A list of people one might aim at: family and friends.
explanation.walkthrough: An Aunt Sally is a British pub and fairground game in which sticks are thrown at a dummy's head, hence a figurative target for criticism.
explanation.definitionFit: An Aunt Sally is anyone set up as an easy object of attack or blame, a butt of criticism.

clue.text: Chapter in St John, maybe, one moving men to great effect

definitions.text: one moving men to great effect

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one letter is placed within a name

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for chapter
St John Fisher was an English bishop and martyr

explanation.surface: A chapter of St John's Gospel, perhaps, featuring a great motivator of people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'St John' points to the Gospel but is the saint John Fisher. 'Men' are chess pieces, which Bobby Fischer moved to great effect.
explanation.definitionFit: Bobby Fischer was an American world chess champion, celebrated for brilliant play with the pieces.

clue.text: Sacked a user, others being kept in one’s place

indicators.note: a sacked town is ransacked and thrown into disorder, so the letters are scattered

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: One employee was fired while the rest held on to their jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sacked' looks like a firing; 'kept in one's place' looks like keeping a job, but means confined to home.
explanation.definitionFit: House arrest confines someone to their own residence under guard rather than in prison.

clue.text: Can’t wait beyond day for scrap

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for day
to itch to do something is to be impatient for it

explanation.surface: Someone is impatient for the day of the fight to arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrap' looks like a fight, fitting the surface, but it is the verb for discard.
explanation.definitionFit: To ditch a plan or object is to discard or abandon it, to get rid of it.

clue.text: It follows bloke around enclosure

indicators.note: lying around something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: a bloke is a he, a male
ENC is the abbreviation for enclosure in a letter

explanation.surface: Something trails a man round a pen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It follows' looks like the subject of the sentence but is the definition, meaning therefore.
explanation.definitionFit: Hence introduces a consequence, meaning therefore or for this reason, as when a conclusion follows logically.

clue.text: Reflecting indeed after Victor’s involved in foul play

indicators.note: to be involved in something is to be caught up inside it, so one letter is placed within
a reflection is a mirror image, so the letters appear back to front
coming after means following behind, so the piece named first is placed second

blocks.note: foul things are unclean
V is Victor in the NATO phonetic alphabet
ay means yes, indeed

explanation.surface: Someone thoughtfully confirms that Victor has been caught up in skulduggery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foul play' reads as one phrase meaning crime, but it splits: 'foul' is wordplay and 'play' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncle Vanya is the Chekhov drama of 1899, a classic of the Russian theatre stage.

clue.text: Annoys head that Pole’s put in for redundancy

indicators.note: something put in is inserted, so a letter is placed between the other pieces

blocks.note: to needle someone is to annoy them
S is the South Pole
a ness is a headland

explanation.surface: A boss is irritated that a Polish worker has been put in during a round of layoffs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Redundancy' suggests job losses, fitting the boss and the worker, but here it is the abstract quality. A ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness's neighbour Dungeness.
explanation.definitionFit: Redundancy means superfluity, being more than is required, which is the condition of being unnecessary.

clue.text: Trying hard to conceal aim with tweet

indicators.note: to conceal something is to hide it inside, so one word goes within another

blocks.note: to train a gun is to aim it
birds tweet when they sing

explanation.surface: Someone works hard at hiding their purpose in a social media post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tweet' looks like a social media post but is birdsong.
explanation.definitionFit: Straining means making great effort, exerting oneself to the limit, as a muscle does.

clue.text: Misery and scandal after blackguard has gone out

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or disordered, so the letters are put in a different order
coming after means following behind, so the piece named first is placed second

blocks.note: a cur is a scoundrel
mud is scandal, as in mudslinging
taken as written

explanation.surface: Wretchedness and disgrace follow once a rogue has left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Misery' looks like unhappiness but is a person: a misery is a moaning killjoy in British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A curmudgeon is a bad-tempered grouch, just as a misery is a constantly gloomy complainer.

clue.text: Dance with married tailor to cause embarrassment

blocks.note: a disco is a dance
M is the abbreviation for married
to tailor something is to fit it

explanation.surface: Dancing with one's wedded spouse and their tailor would make anyone blush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tailor' looks like a person but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To discomfit someone is to unsettle or disconcert them, making them feel awkward and uneasy.

clue.text: Angle to follow in aeroplane manoeuvre

blocks.note: to angle is to fish
to tail someone is to follow them

explanation.surface: A pilot follows a certain angle while performing a manoeuvre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Angle' sounds geometrical, which suits a flight manoeuvre, but it means to go fishing.
explanation.definitionFit: A fishtail is a sideways swinging of an aircraft's tail to lose speed, used when landing.

clue.text: Increasingly wary of strange opening hands

indicators.note: opening something up means prising it apart, so one word slots inside another

blocks.note: eerie means strange and unsettling
left and right hands, L and R

explanation.surface: Someone grows more suspicious of a weird first deal of cards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hands' are the left and right ones; 'opening' is a verb here, not a chess opening or first deal.
explanation.definitionFit: Leery means suspicious or cautious, so leerier is more distrustful, growing in caution.

clue.text: One’s awful blunder on drive, making line on map

blocks.note: I for one, with S for the 's
OG stands for own goal, a dreadful football blunder
to ram something in is to drive it hard

explanation.surface: Someone makes a dreadful error while driving and gets lost on the map.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive' looks like driving a car, and 'blunder on drive' like a motoring error. In the down entry 'on' sets the blunder above the drive.
explanation.definitionFit: An isogram is a contour line on a chart joining points of equal value, such as pressure or temperature.

clue.text: One making 29 yard bursts no fan of hard toil

definitions.note: 29 is AIRDROP, a drop from the sky

indicators.note: to burst into something is to break in, so letters break into the middle of another word

blocks.note: YD is the abbreviation for yard
a skiver is British slang for a shirker who avoids work

explanation.surface: A slacker hates graft yet makes an effort in bursts.
explanation.walkthrough: A skiver is British slang for someone who dodges work. The cross-reference to 29 means an air drop.
explanation.definitionFit: A skydiver jumps from an aircraft and falls through the air, so they make a descent from the heavens.

clue.text: Shy? Did wrong to hold one’s tongue

indicators.note: something gone wrong is out of order, so the letters are put in a new order
to hold something is to keep it inside, so one letter sits within the jumble

blocks.note: both words taken letter for letter
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A timid person who blundered decides to keep quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about staying silent, but 'tongue' is the definition in its sense of a language.
explanation.definitionFit: Yiddish is the language of Ashkenazi Jews, a Germanic tongue written in Hebrew script.

clue.text: Old court to make a fool of as it were?

definitions.text: to make a fool of as it were?

blocks.note: first meaning: the periodic county courts of England and Wales, abolished in 1971

blocks.clueFragment: to make a fool of as it were?
blocks.note: second meaning: a made-up verb, ass plus the suffix -ize, to make an ass of

explanation.walkthrough: The second half invents a verb: adding -ize to ass would mean to turn someone into an ass. 'As it were' and the question mark flag the coinage.

clue.text: Tip trailer, needing something to grip

blocks.note: a trailer for a film is an advertisement, an ad
a vice is a workshop clamp that grips

explanation.surface: Someone tipping a trailer needs something to grab.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip' and 'trailer' suggest dumping a load, but 'Tip' is a hint and the trailer is a film preview. A vice is a bench clamp.
explanation.definitionFit: A tip is a helpful hint or piece of guidance, which is what advice offers.

clue.text: Hit song from Il Trovatore head disliked, somehow

indicators.note: somehow means by some unspecified means, so the letters are rearranged in an unspecified way

blocks.note: all four words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A smash hit from Verdi's opera Il Trovatore that the boss somehow hated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit song from Il Trovatore' sends you to the Anvil Chorus, but only 'Hit song' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Video Killed the Radio Star was the Buggles' chart-topping single of 1979, a famous pop record.

clue.text: Ruin suit

blocks.note: first meaning: to finish someone off
second meaning: to be good enough for, to serve

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruin suit' looks like spoiling clothes; it is two verbs joined by nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both to destroy someone and to be adequate or serve a purpose.

clue.text: Legal permission to broadcast ceremonies

indicators.note: a broadcast is heard over the air, so the word is identified by its sound

blocks.note: legal permissions are entitlements under the law

explanation.surface: A licence to televise a solemn ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests broadcasting rights; 'to broadcast' is the cue to say the word aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: Rites are formal religious or solemn acts performed in a set order, like a funeral or wedding.

clue.text: Missing uniform marred retinue fit for a queen

indicators.note: something missing is absent, so a letter is removed
something marred is damaged and spoilt, so the letters are knocked out of order

blocks.note: both words taken letter for letter
U is Uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Without matching costumes, a messy train of attendants looks fine for royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit for a queen' is a stock phrase, but 'fit' is fodder and 'a queen' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Nefertiti was the Egyptian royal consort of Pharaoh Akhenaten, famed for her painted bust.

clue.text: Daily charge hitting the roof?

blocks.note: the i is a British daily newspaper
a rate is a charge, as in a fee

explanation.surface: A daily fee that goes through the ceiling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily charge' reads as a per-day fee, but the daily is the i, a British national newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: To hit the roof is an idiom for flying into a rage, so someone doing it is furious.

clue.text: Change ending of popular film — oddly shocking treatment!

indicators.note: oddly here means in the odd positions, so only the first and third letters are kept

blocks.note: in means popular, fashionable
the first and third letters
ECT is electroconvulsive therapy, an electric shock treatment

explanation.surface: A hit movie's finale is rewritten, a strangely shocking way to treat it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change ending of popular film' reads as a director's cut, but only the first three words define, in the grammatical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammatically, to inflect a word is to alter its form, typically its suffix, to show tense, number or case.

clue.text: Fancy putting answer forward without digressing

indicators.note: putting something elsewhere lifts it from its place, so a letter is removed before being set down again
moving forward means going to the front, so the lifted letter now leads

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for answer
a dream is a fancy

explanation.surface: An imagined way to push one's reply forward without wandering off topic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forward' says where the moved letter goes: the A in the dream moves to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Ad rem is Latin for to the matter, meaning relevant and keeping to the point at hand.

clue.text: Finally taking a very short vacation, acquiring fuel

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the closing letter is kept
something short is cut down, so only the opening letters are kept

blocks.note: the closing letter
taken as written
so means very, as in so good
hol is a British shortening of holiday, a vacation

explanation.surface: At last someone gets a brief break and fills up the tank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very short' reads as one phrase about a brief trip, but it splits: 'very' gives a word, and 'short' trims the holiday.
explanation.definitionFit: Gasohol is motor fuel blending petrol with ethanol alcohol, used to power cars.

clue.text: Uncle Sam pauses to drop one off on time

indicators.note: dropping something lets it fall away, so a letter is left out

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
to hesitate is to pause
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: An American hesitates to drop someone off on time.
explanation.walkthrough: Uncle Sam looks like a person in the scene, but he personifies the USA.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncle Sam is the national personification of the USA, standing for America as a whole.
